extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of moral philosophy and intellectual history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and assessing the distinctive ethical criteria and practical prescriptions of Stoicism (and contrasted ancient schools) as presented in a historical/philosophical survey. Focuses on virtues, motives, education, social duty, and theological/ethical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as the sole real good
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that 'there is no real good but virtue' — virtue alone is the true good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads Stoics to deny argument for a future world based on reward/punishment; implies acting from duty regardless of external recompense. Example: Stoics contend 'a good man should act irrespectively of reward.' Practical consequence: ethics centered entirely on internal moral quality rather than external goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting from duty irrespective of reward
rubrics_metrics.description: A good action is to be performed for its own sake, not for praise or future reward ('do his duty, and to tell the truth').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stoic precepts emphasise self-sacrifice and refusal to make praise the end of right. Anti-pattern: doing good primarily to gain fame or posthumous reputation. Example aphorisms: 'Nothing for opinion, all for conscience.'; 'He who wishes his virtue to be blazed abroad is not labouring for virtue but for fame.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression of the affections; ascendancy of reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete subordination or suppression of emotions to give absolute ascendancy to reason; affections are treated as diseases or perturbations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stoicism aims to 'repress manifest and acknowledged desires' and to make the will govern conduct. Consequence: emotions like pity are condemned as weakening judgment. Anti-pattern: allowing unregulated emotion to drive action rather than dispassionate judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will-based merit versus spontaneous benevolence
rubrics_metrics.description: Merit is attached primarily to actions of the will performed against natural inclination, rather than to spontaneous kindly feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two character types: (1) will-dominated persons whose virtue costs effort (highest merit), and (2) persons naturally disposed to virtue whose spontaneity wins affection. Stoics value the former for merit, though the latter attracts more love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education: strengthen the will versus guide the desires
rubrics_metrics.description: Two distinct educational aims — (a) systems (Spartan/Stoic/ascetic) that strengthen the will to endure and repress desires; (b) systems that make virtue attractive, guiding desires toward virtuous ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose method depending on social conditions: will-strengthening suits disturbed/military societies; making virtue attractive suits tranquil, organised civilisations. Practical implication: curricula and moral pedagogy should be tailored to character types and social needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clemency as reasoned virtue; pity as vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Clemency is an act of judgment (gentleness in punishment) and a high virtue; pity is unreasoning emotion that disturbs judgment and is therefore a vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seneca's distinction: clemency adjudicates proportion between suffering and guilt; pity contemplates only suffering. Stoic practice: help the worthy without emotional disturbance; avoid 'weeping with' those who weep. Anti-pattern: allowing pity to override justice or reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impersonal, reasoned philanthropy (fraternity of all men)
rubrics_metrics.description: A duty of universal brotherhood to be enacted through reasoned, passionless benevolence that seeks the welfare of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stoics expand the sphere of charity by principle rather than sympathy; they may even extend compassion toward criminals by treating guilt as ignorance. Practical prescription: labour for welfare of mankind dispassionately; motivation is duty, not sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment justified only for prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopting Plato's paradox that 'all guilt is ignorance,' Stoics treat crime as involuntary disease and assert that the legitimate ground for punishment is prevention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reframes penal policy toward correction and deterrence rather than retribution. Anti-pattern: punitive systems motivated by vengeance or moral outrage rather than prevention and reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality/identity of virtues; no gradations
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrines that 'all virtues are equal' or 'are the same' and likewise that 'all vices are equal'; Stoic tendency to deny gradations of virtue or vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to rigid moral judgments and a lack of nuanced assessment of different moral qualities. Practical consequence: system ill-suited to ordinary mixed motives; tends to produce extremes in moral prescription and difficulty accommodating common human behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to nature as the measure of virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is conformity to nature; reason is the directing power and highest faculty of an intelligent being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stoics elevate reason as normative; but Lecky criticises the reduction of 'the higher part' to the whole, calling it a mutilation of humanity. Implication: normative claims should account for the composite nature of human faculties (reason + emotions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignity of man: pride (inner approbation) vs vanity (external)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pride — self-approbation derived from virtue — is permissible and central in Stoicism; vanity — seeking others' opinion — is condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral self-respect (pride) is a chief Stoic motive; caution against transforming pride into narcissistic separation from social obligations. Example: 'Pride... was not only permitted in Stoicism, it was even its leading moral agent.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of the Divine and submission to Providence
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is represented as imitating God; an attitude of absolute submission to Providence is incumbent on the Stoic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical maxims: accept losses as restorations, perform whatever social role 'the Master has ordained.' Balances human dignity with humility before cosmic order. Risk: such submission can slide into quietism incompatible with active virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active political duty and patriotism as central moral obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Patriotism and public/political activity are high moral duties; 'all virtue is in action' — moral life is practical and civic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stoicism historically encouraged political engagement (e.g., Marcus Aurelius). Moral systems should accommodate public service as essential expression of virtue. Anti-pattern: extreme withdrawal from civic life (quietism) when virtue is preached only as inner discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation for death through meditation
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent meditation on death to detach from worldly goods and diminish terrors of death; 'continually meditating on death' as mental discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aims to produce equanimity toward loss and to strengthen self-control. Lecky warns of overemphasis: excessive preoccupation may produce a 'tense, feverish, and tragical character' and undermine living well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death regarded as natural rest; absence of penal character
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient philosophers commonly regarded death as a neutral or beneficent 'rest' rather than a penal or supernatural punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical consolation literature ('Consolations') uses death as a motive for courage, not punishment. Practical note: denying penal afterlife weakens incentives based on future reward/punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation and posthumous fame as moral incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire for reputation, especially posthumous fame, was a strong moral spring in Roman morality and influenced rhetoric and conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stoics warn against making fame the end of virtue; practice should resist ostentation. Lecky notes theatrical phraseology stemming from the prominence of reputation among Roman moralists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral self-reliance: looking for good/evil in oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoic maxim that the wise man 'looks for all his good and evil from himself' — moral responsibility and resourcefulness are internal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fosters autonomy and firmness in adversity. Risk: may lead to overconfidence and neglect of dependence on community or divine assistance; balanced systems temper self-reliance with social duties and humility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of extirpating emotions: mutilation of humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical standard: a moral system that extirpates emotions to privilege reason alone mutilates human nature and produces grave evils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky's judgment: reasoned suppression of affective springs undermines true benevolence; ethical frameworks should respect a composite human nature and preserve emotions that motivate caring behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability threshold: Stoicism fit for heroic few, not masses
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoicism's high standard of self-control and absence of gradations makes it unsuitable for the majority of people and ordinary conditions of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy/education implication: adopt moral systems that can influence mixed motives and common characters; heroic-only systems risk being impractical and rejected by the multitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of quietism from absolute submission
rubrics_metrics.description: A doctrine of absolute submission to Providence and proscription of affections risks producing quietism incompatible with active moral and political life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical mitigation: ancient emphasis on civic duty prevented wholesale quietism. Contemporary designers of ethical systems should guard against doctrines that undercut social engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical neglect of natural science
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoical disdain for studies other than virtue led to neglect of physical science, limiting the school's corrective impact on ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral systems benefit from integrating empirical knowledge; failing to correct ignorance of nature can retard social and intellectual progress. Anti-pattern: moral teaching that dismisses empirical inquiry.
